lesson.child_mission: Debugging finds why a program misbehaves: read the steps, reproduce the bug, form a fix hypothesis, change one thing, retest.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Your sprite walks through a wall. Give two possible causes and a test for one.

FEEDBACK
e.g. missing collision check; wrong coordinates — test by adding a wall condition.

WATCH FOR
Changing many lines at once makes the fix mysterious.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Debug three broken sample programs (teacher-provided or peer). Bug diary with hypothesis, change and result for each.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Debugging finds why a program misbehaves: read the steps, reproduce the bug, form a fix hypothesis, change one thing, retest.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Debug three broken sample programs (teacher-provided or peer). Bug diary with hypothesis, change and result for each. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Likely misconception: Changing many lines at once makes the fix mysterious. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about debug, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

WORKED MODEL

TRY FIRST

FEEDBACK

teach_steps.explain:
Debugging finds why a program misbehaves: read the steps, reproduce the bug, form a fix hypothesis, change one thing, retest.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
